records.mutation: lead with counting how many partners each branch leaves open, and recast a collapsed branch as eliminated-by-the-statement rather than a contradiction to resolve
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent scored 1/8; 2 truncated and every rollout burned 14k-16.4k tokens. Six failures fixed the multiplicative reading, enumerated its factor pairs, then noticed a speaker's own value pins the partner uniquely there, called that a contradiction, and spent thousands of tokens trying to resolve it before reporting a factor they had already refuted or admitted was recalled from a classic puzzle. The lone success skipped enumeration entirely and reasoned about how many partners remain open under the additive reading. The incumbent tells the student to intersect constraints across live readings, but the student never gets that far because it treats a collapsed branch as broken rather than as evidence deleting that branch, so I made counting-partners-per-branch the first move and recast collapse as elimination.

records.mutation: reorder verification discipline so the simplified value is recorded before any checking, and require naming the exact wrong line before abandoning a derivation
records.subagent_summary: Seven of eight rollouts were correct in 5.8k-9.1k tokens; the failure derived the correct locus and center/radius by 3k tokens, then mis-evaluated a reciprocal of a purely imaginary number while spot-checking one root, and because it had not yet written any result down it spent the remaining 13k tokens re-auditing a sound derivation and finally doubting the substitution itself, ending with nothing stated. Rounds 5-8 all tried to bound or repair that audit loop and lost transfer; the incumbent already says to state the result early but buries that clause last, after the recheck advice. So I reorder the discipline: record the simplified value the moment it exists, verify only afterwards with whatever room remains, and require pointing at a specific wrong line before abandoning anything.

records.mutation: replace abstract bound-plus-witness with a concrete symmetric-case-plus-perturbation substitute for the angle sweep, add a repeat-what-if stop trigger, and end on a three-line no-headings write-up rule
records.subagent_summary: Two of eight scored. All eight found the value early (first 3-6k of ~55-63k chars), so the wedge and inclusion-exclusion advice works; every failure was budget, not math. Three never closed reasoning at all, still numerically re-testing rotation angles (98-205 rotation mentions, 45-82 restarts). Three did close reasoning but then spent all remaining tokens re-arguing from scratch why the symmetric configuration is minimal, restating the setup, and were cut off before any result appeared. The incumbent bound-plus-witness clause is too abstract to trigger and its transcribe rule is buried, so this revision gives a concrete substitute for the parameter sweep (evaluate the most symmetric case, then a perturbation argument), a checkable stop trigger (a repeat what-if means halt), and moves the short-write-up rule to the end where it is acted on.

records.mutation: pin the residual at the piece's full degree d (subtracting an affine part cannot drop it to d-1) and replace the open audit with commit-and-stop once the bound is proved
records.subagent_summary: 3 of 8 fresh rollouts were correct and the pointwise-residual plus reusability framing is clearly landing: every finisher reached the summed m*d budget shape. The dominant error has shifted to degree bookkeeping - three rollouts asserted the residual has degree d-1 after subtracting the affine part and so reported a budget one factor short per piece. One reverted to the old trap of forcing a single piece to step by a constant and concluded each piece serves exactly one index; one hit the token limit after already deriving the right count, then relitigating it. So the revision adds one sentence stating that subtracting an affine part leaves the leading term untouched, so the residual keeps the FULL degree and never d-1, and replaces the open-ended audit with an instruction to state the count once the bound is proved and not reopen it.

records.mutation: replace the vague discard-degenerate clause with substitute-to-test roots plus a reversal rule when the kept root degenerates
records.subagent_summary: Seven of eight fresh rollouts were correct at about 9k tokens; the single failure reduced correctly to the right two-root equation, then screened the roots against a domain interval it recalled wrongly, threw away the admissible one, kept the root that collapsed the figure, and reported that collapsed value as its result instead of reading the collapse as a signal. The incumbent tells the student to discard degenerate or out-of-domain roots but gives no way to tell them apart, which is exactly the ambiguity that bit here. I sharpened just that clause: test each root by substituting it rather than trusting a remembered rule, and treat a degenerate survivor as proof the other root was correct. Everything else stays terse, since brevity is the only edit that has ever gained transfer for this hint.

records.mutation: state that a pile bottom is the FIRST delivery (not the item delivered last) and legitimize two parts sharing the same value so the student stops abandoning the shared atom set on the later part
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent gave 1/8; six rollouts stopped normally at 12k-15k tokens and two hit the cap, so length is secondary. Six of the eight reached the 2^(free) atom count on the first part and then abandoned it on the second, asserting every item is equally likely in every slot and reading off 1/n or 1/2; five of those also equated the requested bottom slot with the item delivered last, and the one correct rollout got there only by keeping the same atom set for both parts, so the two parts coincided. The revision keeps the shared free-step sample space, replaces the vague first-vs-last hedge with the concrete rule that a pile bottom is its FIRST delivery, bans pricing a slot-occupancy event as 1/n, and states outright that two parts may honestly share one value so a repeat is not a reason to switch methods.

records.mutation: add a formula-vs-hand-solved-instance consistency check, an abort rule for reformulations needing unpinnable constants or long products, and a block on the underdetermined/guess-zero escapes
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling scored 2 of 8. Both successes solved the three smallest instances by plain elimination, read off the signed reciprocal-factorial pattern, and landed. All six failures instead recast the setup as a polynomial with a product factor times an undetermined linear factor: five ran to the token cap trying to pin two unknown constants from one condition, and one closed on a wrong value after an unverified coefficient extraction. Two explicitly concluded the system was underdetermined and one committed to zero out of exhaustion, even though the conditions are square and independent. The revision therefore keeps commit-then-verify, adds a mandatory check of any general formula against a hand-solved smallest instance, tells the student to drop a reformulation as soon as it needs a symmetric function, a long product, or an unpinnable constant, and blocks the underdetermined and guess-zero exits.

records.mutation: keep the train-safe opening and small-cases clause verbatim; replace the exact-arithmetic clause with a change-of-representation escalation (condition-to-equation, complementary counting, choose the most-constrained variable)
records.subagent_summary: All 8 fresh rollouts scored reward 1 with clean stops, so train_i is pinned at 1.0 and every gain must come from transfer. The rollouts never invoke exact-fraction or simplify-late reasoning at all (zero occurrences), so that clause is dead weight; what they actually burn tokens on is 5-25 self-interruptions per rollout re-deriving the same arithmetic in the same framing, up to 6.6k tokens. Nine rounds of evidence say the opening must stay verbatim (every wholesale rewrite crashed train to 0.25-0.5) and that only the tail sentence is safe to change. Round 9's tail edit (exact products plus substitute-back) lost transfer, so instead of another arithmetic-hygiene rule I swapped in a second-tier escalation: if the first attack stalls, switch representation rather than grind harder.

records.mutation: compress the centered-ansatz core and spend the freed tokens on generic output discipline: keep values exact rather than decimal, simplify, and emit exactly the requested quantity in the requested form and order
records.subagent_summary: All 8 fresh rollouts were correct and every one stopped cleanly at 3.8k-8.8k tokens, so the incumbent has fully eliminated the budget-exhaustion and ansatz-mis-parameterization failures that dominated rounds 1-8; there is no remaining training failure to target. Successes matched a common shape: commit to the shared-center antisymmetric pair, solve the two data values by sum and difference, then evaluate inside the centered form. Since train is saturated and transfer is weighted double, the revision preserves that proven core verbatim in meaning but compresses its wording, and reinvests the freed tokens in guidance that fires on every problem rather than only on this narrow commuting-map pattern: keep quantities exact instead of decimal, simplify, and report precisely the quantity requested in the requested form and order.

records.mutation: pin unit-of-iteration (whole sequence, not a single step) alongside the block-slide scope, and rewrite the block rule as a rigid N-place shift preserving current internal order
records.subagent_summary: 3 of 8 scored; the 5 failures split into two mechanical jams, both upstream of any reasoning about order. Two rollouts spent thousands of tokens relitigating whether one application was the entire listed sequence or a single step, then counted intermediate rows as returns and got a count too small. Three others mis-executed the block move: they wrote each block back in its original internal order rather than its current scrambled order, so their traces stopped being rearrangements of the previous row, disagreed with their own structural claims, and looped on 'this is confusing' until the cap. All five also fell back on disjoint-transposition talk to assert period two. The incumbent scopes the block move but never fixes the unit of iteration and never says the block travels rigidly, so the revision pins both up front and keeps the terse commit clause.
